title: Count the cost first
hookLine: before you begin anything, look at what comes first and what follows, like an athlete before the games (Enchiridion 29)
last: WHO HANDED YOU OVER? — MY MIND IS MINE.

lines: NEW SHOES, STILL IN THE BOX.
A FEW WEEKS LATER: THE CLOSET.
cards: New running shoes, still in the box. A water bottle with the hours printed down the side. A plan taped to the fridge.

A few weeks later, the shoes are in the closet. The wanting didn't stop. The plan was all beginning and no middle: nobody pictured the five-forty alarm in the dark, the sore knees, the Thursday that didn't feel like it.
Section twenty-nine of the handbook is about that missing middle, and it uses an athlete to show it.

teach.b: In every undertaking, Epictetus says, look at what comes before it and what follows from it, and only then set about it. Otherwise you'll start eagerly, and later, when the hard parts show up, you'll give up in shame.
Then the athlete. You want to win at Olympia? So do I, he says; it's a fine thing.

But look at what comes first. A strict routine, eating on a schedule, no sweets, training at set hours in heat and cold, no cold water and no wine when you're told not to, handing yourself to the trainer as to a doctor.

teach.h: THE ATHLETE: DIET, DUST, A BEATING.
teach.b: Then in the contest you may dislocate a wrist, twist an ankle, swallow a lot of dust, take a beating, and after all that, lose.

Skip the counting, he says, and you'll be like children who play wrestlers, then gladiators, then trumpeters, then actors, trying everything and finishing nothing. Weigh it all, and if you still want it, go ahead.

The same picture appears in the Gospel of Luke, about following Jesus, in the King James words: "For which of you, intending to build a tower, sitteth not down first, and counteth the cost, whether he have sufficient to finish it?"

A different teacher, a different calling, the same sitting down before you start. Epictetus isn't trying to scare anyone off. People who have already seen the middle are better placed to get through it.

how: Some Stoic practitioners, before taking on something new, picture its demands and setbacks in detail and only then decide whether to begin.

look at what comes first and what follows, then decide.
games.why: weigh the diet, the training, the dust and the chance of losing, he says; then, if you still want it, go ahead.

practice: Choose one plan you're about to start, and walk past the easy beginning into the middle: what will the third week ask, what will you give up, where will it get boring or hard?
See it plainly, the way Epictetus lists the dust and the twisted ankle. Then ask whether you still want it, and notice the answer.

wordCard.voice: Olympia. Where the games Epictetus describes were held: look at what comes before and what follows, like an athlete training for them, then begin. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek, Enchiridion 29: the Olympic games, at Olympia.
